demo_steps.title: All four bonds are identical
demo_steps.narration: In the ball-and-stick model, all four C–H rods are the same length and meet at the same 109.5° angle. The tetrahedra on the left show the same geometry. The flat notation is just one frozen view of this shape.

demo_steps.title: Bonds in the plane of the page

demo_steps.title: Bond receding into the page
demo_steps.narration: The left H is reached by a dashed line. The dashes encode that this bond points away from the viewer, behind the page surface. The matching rod in the model tilts backward.

demo_steps.title: Bond coming out of the page
demo_steps.narration: The bottom H sits on a heavy black wedge that widens away from C. The wedge means this bond projects toward the viewer, out of the page. The matching rod in the model tilts forward.

Flat 2D layout, world X spans [-6, 6], Y spans [-2.5, 2.5]. Three non-overlapping horizontal panels:

LEFT PANEL (x ∈ [-5.5, -2.5]): Two magenta tetrahedra side by side. Each tetrahedron edge length ~1.2 world units. First tetrahedron centered at (-4.5, 0.3, 0): four vertices forming a triangular outline visible from a three-quarter view, all edges magenta #d6198a line-width 2, except one front-lower edge drawn with line-width 5 (thick). Second tetrahedron centered at (-3.0, 0.3, 0): same magenta outline, plus one solid black line (#111111, width 2) from top vertex to center-front and one dashed black line from right vertex to center. Caption 'A regular tetrahedron' at y = -1.5, centered under both.

CENTER PANEL (x ∈ [-1.5, 1.5]): Letter 'C' at origin (0, 0). H above at (0, 1.2) connected by thin line. H right at (1.2, 0) connected by thin line. H left at (-1.2, 0) connected by dashed line (3 dashes). H below at (0, -1.2) connected by a filled black wedge triangle widening from C (width 0.05 at C) to H (width 0.35 at H). Leader arrows: 'Bonds in plane of page' arrow points to top-right area; 'Bond receding into page' arrow points left; 'Bond coming out of plane' arrow points down. Labels placed outside the bond region.

RIGHT PANEL (x ∈ [2.5, 5.5]): Ball-and-stick model centered at (4.0, 0.3, 0). Carbon sphere radius 0.35, color #4a4a4a, MeshStandardMaterial with roughness 0.4. Four H spheres radius 0.22, color #e8e8d8, at tetrahedral positions (109.5° angles) distance 1.0 from center. Rods radius 0.04, color #cccccc, MeshStandardMaterial. One directional light from upper-left and ambient light for shading. Curly brace spanning x ∈ [-1.5, 5.5] at y = -1.8. Caption 'A tetrahedral carbon atom' at y = -2.2 centered under brace.

Highlight color: gold #ffcc00 applied to matching bonds/rods. Non-highlighted elements dim to 30% opacity when a specific category is selected.
plan.notes: Use axis_screen_angles: null for a purely front-on 2D rendering. All elements are flat geometry (lines, triangles, circles/spheres rendered front-on). Use MeshStandardMaterial with a DirectionalLight (intensity 1.2, position [2, 3, 4]) and AmbientLight (intensity 0.5) so spheres read as solid 3D objects. The wedge bond is a filled triangle mesh (THREE.Shape + ShapeGeometry). Dashed lines use LineDashedMaterial. Captions and labels use a single system (addLabel or SVG text, not both) to avoid duplication. On state change, set material emissive to gold on highlighted elements and reduce opacity of non-highlighted ones. The tetrahedron thick edge must be a single edge of the tetrahedron (connecting two of its four vertices), not a separate horizontal bar.

authoredPrompt: This figure sets a geometric solid beside a chemical structure to establish a drawing convention, using four images across one horizontal band. At the left are two magenta line drawings of a four-faced solid: the first a plain outline with one front edge thickened, the second adding black interior edges, one solid and one dashed, that run from the top vertex and a side vertex to the center. The pair is labeled "A regular tetrahedron". At the right, a carbon written as "C" carries four hydrogens written as "H": one directly above and one to the right on ordinary thin lines, one to the left on a short dashed line, and one below on a heavy black wedge that widens away from the carbon. Three leader arrows name these bond types as "Bonds in plane of page", "Bond receding into page", and "Bond coming out of plane". A ball-and-stick model at the far right shows a dark gray central sphere with four pale hydrogen spheres on light rods, and a curly brace groups the notation and the model under "A tetrahedral carbon atom". Aligning solid, flat notation, and model lets the reader read wedges and dashes as depth cues rather than as different kinds of bonds, the shorthand used for three-dimensional structures throughout organic chemistry.
authoredInteractions: - Click for selecting Bonds in plane of page, Bond receding into page, or Bond coming out of plane; the chosen leader label, bond mark, and corresponding 3D bond glow together, clarifying that the marks encode orientation rather than different bond types.
authoredContext:
A representation of a tetrahedral carbon atom is shown in the figure. Note the conventions used to show three-dimensionality: solid lines represent bonds in the plane of the page, the heavy wedged line represents a bond coming out of the page toward the viewer, and the dashed line represents a bond receding back behind the page, away from the viewer. Get used to them; these representations will be used throughout the text.

A representation of van’t Hoff’s tetrahedral carbon atom. The solid lines represent bonds in the plane of the paper, the heavy wedged line represents a bond coming out of the plane of the page toward the viewer, and the dashed line represents a bond going back behind the plane of the page away from the viewer.

Two regular tetrahedrons (one with 3 D representation), the wedge-bond structure, and ball and stick model of a tetrahedral carbon atom.

Why, though, do atoms bond together, and how can chemical bonds be described electronically? The why question is relatively easy to answer: atoms bond together because the compound that results is more stable and lower in energy than the separate atoms. Energy—usually as heat—is always released and flows out of the chemical system when a bond forms. Conversely, energy is added to the chemical system when a bond breaks. Making bonds always releases energy, and breaking bonds always absorbs energy. The how question is more difficult. To answer it, we need to know more about the electronic properties of atoms.
